chapter_text:
CHAPTER 17 - COORDINATION AND CONTROL: THE NERVOUS AND ENDOCRINE SYSTEMS

Introduction

The human body is made of trillions of cells organised into tissues, organs and organ systems. For the body to work as a single, smoothly functioning unit, the activities of all these parts must be linked together and regulated. This linking and regulation is called COORDINATION. When you touch a hot object your hand pulls back at once; when you run, your heart beats faster, your breathing deepens and your muscles receive extra glucose. Such precisely timed, cooperative responses are possible only because two great control systems work together: the NERVOUS SYSTEM, which gives rapid, short-lived, electrical control, and the ENDOCRINE SYSTEM, which gives slower, longer-lasting, chemical control through hormones. This chapter describes the structure and working of both systems and compares the two kinds of control.

17.1 THE NEED FOR COORDINATION

Living cells constantly receive information about changes in their internal and external environment. A change that produces a response is called a STIMULUS (for example light, sound, heat, pressure or a chemical). The structures that detect stimuli are RECEPTORS (such as the eye, ear, skin and taste buds), and the structures that carry out the response are EFFECTORS (mainly muscles and glands). Coordination is the process that connects receptors to effectors so that the correct response follows the right stimulus at the right time. In animals this is achieved by the nervous system and the endocrine system acting together. Without coordination the many organs would act independently and the body could not survive.

17.2 THE NERVOUS SYSTEM: THE NEURON

The nervous system is built from billions of specialised cells called NEURONS (nerve cells), the structural and functional units of the nervous system. Between neurons lie supporting cells called NEUROGLIA (glial cells) that nourish, insulate and protect them. A typical neuron has three parts. (1) The CELL BODY (cyton or soma) contains the nucleus and most of the cytoplasm with its organelles; granular structures called Nissl granules are found here. (2) DENDRITES are short, branched fibres that project from the cell body and RECEIVE impulses, carrying them TOWARDS the cell body. (3) The AXON is a single long fibre that carries impulses AWAY from the cell body towards the next neuron or an effector. Many axons are wrapped in a fatty insulating layer called the MYELIN SHEATH, formed by Schwann cells. The myelin sheath is interrupted at intervals by gaps called the NODES OF RANVIER. Myelin insulates the axon and greatly speeds up impulse conduction. The junction across which one neuron communicates with the next neuron (or with a muscle) is called a SYNAPSE; the two cells do not actually touch but are separated by a tiny gap, the synaptic cleft.

Neurons are classified by function into three types. SENSORY (afferent) neurons carry impulses from receptors to the central nervous system. MOTOR (efferent) neurons carry impulses from the central nervous system to effectors (muscles and glands). INTERNEURONS (association or relay neurons), found within the brain and spinal cord, connect sensory and motor neurons. A NERVE is a bundle of many axons bound together by connective tissue.

17.3 THE NERVE IMPULSE

A neuron carries information as an electrical signal called the NERVE IMPULSE, which travels along the membrane of the axon. In a resting (unstimulated) neuron the inside of the membrane is negatively charged relative to the outside; this potential difference of about -70 millivolts across the membrane is the RESTING POTENTIAL. It is maintained by the SODIUM-POTASSIUM PUMP, which actively pushes sodium ions (Na+) out of the cell and potassium ions (K+) in, keeping the outside rich in Na+ and positively charged. This resting, charged state is described as POLARISED.

When a neuron is stimulated strongly enough (above a threshold), the permeability of the membrane suddenly changes. Sodium channels open and Na+ rushes IN, so that region of the membrane briefly becomes positive inside - this reversal of charge is called DEPOLARISATION and produces the ACTION POTENTIAL. Immediately afterwards potassium channels open, K+ moves OUT, and the original resting charge is restored - this recovery is REPOLARISATION. The action potential travels as a wave along the axon: each depolarised patch triggers depolarisation of the next patch, so the impulse moves without weakening. The nerve impulse obeys the ALL-OR-NONE law: a stimulus either reaches threshold and produces a full impulse, or it does not fire at all. In MYELINATED axons the impulse cannot pass through the insulating myelin and therefore JUMPS from one node of Ranvier to the next; this jumping conduction is called SALTATORY CONDUCTION and makes the impulse travel much faster than in unmyelinated fibres.

SYNAPTIC TRANSMISSION: When an impulse reaches the end of an axon it must cross the synapse to reach the next neuron. The signal cannot leap the gap electrically, so it is carried chemically. The arrival of the impulse causes tiny sacs (vesicles) in the axon ending to release chemical messengers called NEUROTRANSMITTERS (for example acetylcholine) into the synaptic cleft. The neurotransmitter diffuses across the gap and binds to receptors on the membrane of the next neuron, generating a new impulse there. The neurotransmitter is then quickly broken down or reabsorbed so the synapse is ready for the next signal. Synapses ensure that impulses travel in ONE direction only and act as junctions where signals can be passed on, blocked or redirected.

17.4 THE HUMAN NERVOUS SYSTEM

The human nervous system is divided into the CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM (CNS) and the PERIPHERAL NERVOUS SYSTEM (PNS). The CNS consists of the BRAIN and the SPINAL CORD; it processes information and issues commands. The PNS consists of all the nerves that connect the CNS to the rest of the body.

THE BRAIN is the master coordinating organ, protected by the skull and by three membranes called MENINGES, and cushioned by CEREBROSPINAL FLUID. It has three main regions. (1) The FOREBRAIN, dominated by the CEREBRUM, is the largest part; its folded outer layer (the cerebral cortex) controls thinking, memory, reasoning, intelligence, will, voluntary actions and the interpretation of sensations from the sense organs. Within the forebrain lie the THALAMUS, which relays incoming sensory impulses to the cerebrum, and the HYPOTHALAMUS, which controls body temperature, hunger, thirst, sleep, emotions and links the nervous system to the endocrine system by controlling the pituitary gland. (2) The MIDBRAIN connects the forebrain and hindbrain and handles some reflexes of the eyes and ears. (3) The HINDBRAIN includes the CEREBELLUM, which maintains posture, balance and the precise coordination of muscular movements, and the MEDULLA OBLONGATA, which controls involuntary vital activities such as heartbeat, breathing, blood pressure, swallowing, coughing and vomiting.

THE SPINAL CORD is a cylindrical bundle of nerve tissue running down the backbone from the medulla, protected by the vertebral column. It conducts impulses to and from the brain and is the coordinating centre for spinal reflex actions.

THE PERIPHERAL NERVOUS SYSTEM is made of nerves arising from the brain (12 pairs of CRANIAL NERVES) and from the spinal cord (31 pairs of SPINAL NERVES). Functionally the PNS has two divisions. The SOMATIC nervous system carries impulses to the skeletal (voluntary) muscles and controls conscious, voluntary actions. The AUTONOMIC nervous system controls involuntary actions of internal organs, glands and smooth muscle, and itself has two opposing parts. The SYMPATHETIC division prepares the body for emergency, 'fight-or-flight' situations: it speeds up the heartbeat, widens the pupils, raises blood pressure and diverts blood to the muscles. The PARASYMPATHETIC division restores calm 'rest-and-digest' conditions: it slows the heartbeat, constricts the pupils and promotes digestion. The two work antagonistically to keep internal conditions balanced.

17.5 REFLEX ACTION AND THE REFLEX ARC

A REFLEX ACTION is a sudden, automatic, involuntary response to a stimulus that does not require conscious thought - for example the immediate withdrawal of the hand from a hot object, blinking when an object nears the eye, or the knee-jerk. Reflexes protect the body from harm because they are extremely fast. The nerve pathway followed by the impulse during a reflex is called the REFLEX ARC. In a typical reflex arc the components are: RECEPTOR (detects the stimulus, e.g. skin) -> SENSORY NEURON (carries the impulse to the spinal cord) -> INTERNEURON in the spinal cord (relays the impulse) -> MOTOR NEURON (carries the response impulse) -> EFFECTOR (a muscle or gland that produces the response). Because the impulse is processed in the SPINAL CORD rather than the brain, the response is very rapid; the brain is informed only afterwards, which is why we feel the pain a moment after the hand has already been pulled away.

17.6 THE SENSE ORGANS

Sense organs contain receptors that detect stimuli and pass the information to the brain. The main sense organs are the eye (sight), ear (hearing and balance), nose (smell), tongue (taste) and skin (touch).

THE EYE is the organ of sight. Its wall has three layers: the outer SCLERA (protective; its transparent front part is the CORNEA), the middle CHOROID (containing blood vessels; its front forms the coloured IRIS with the PUPIL opening) and the inner RETINA, which carries the light-sensitive cells - RODS (for dim light and black-and-white vision) and CONES (for bright light and colour vision). Light enters through the cornea and pupil; the amount of light is adjusted by the iris; the LENS focuses the light onto the retina, forming a small, inverted, real image. The receptor cells convert light into nerve impulses that travel along the OPTIC NERVE to the cerebrum, where the image is interpreted the right way up.

THE EAR is the organ of hearing and of balance. It has three parts. The OUTER EAR (pinna and ear canal) collects sound waves and directs them to the eardrum (tympanum), which vibrates. The MIDDLE EAR contains three tiny bones (ear ossicles - malleus, incus and stapes) that amplify these vibrations and pass them on. The INNER EAR contains the fluid-filled COCHLEA, whose receptor cells convert the vibrations into nerve impulses sent along the AUDITORY NERVE to the brain for hearing; the inner ear also contains the SEMICIRCULAR CANALS, which help maintain balance and posture.

17.7 THE ENDOCRINE SYSTEM AND HORMONES

The second control system is the ENDOCRINE SYSTEM, made up of ductless glands that pour their secretions directly into the blood. These chemical messengers are called HORMONES. Glands are of two kinds: EXOCRINE glands (such as salivary and sweat glands) release their products through DUCTS, whereas ENDOCRINE glands are DUCTLESS and release hormones straight into the bloodstream, which carries them to distant TARGET ORGANS. A hormone is an organic chemical, secreted in tiny amounts, that regulates the activity of specific target cells. Hormonal control is SLOWER to begin than nervous control but its effects are more WIDESPREAD and longer-lasting. Hormones regulate growth, development, metabolism, reproduction and the internal balance of the body (homeostasis).

17.8 MAJOR ENDOCRINE GLANDS AND THEIR HORMONES

THE PITUITARY GLAND, a pea-sized gland attached to the base of the brain below the hypothalamus, is called the MASTER GLAND because its hormones control several other endocrine glands. It secretes GROWTH HORMONE (which controls growth of the body), hormones that stimulate the thyroid, adrenal cortex and gonads, and other hormones. Its own activity is directed by the hypothalamus.

THE THYROID GLAND, located in the neck in front of the windpipe, secretes THYROXINE, a hormone that contains IODINE and controls the rate of metabolism, growth and development. Its secretion needs an adequate supply of iodine in the diet.

THE PARATHYROID GLANDS, four small glands embedded in the thyroid, secrete PARATHORMONE (parathyroid hormone), which regulates the level of calcium and phosphorus in the blood.

THE ADRENAL GLANDS sit one above each kidney. The inner part (medulla) secretes ADRENALINE (epinephrine), the 'emergency' or 'fight-or-flight' hormone, which raises the heartbeat, breathing rate and blood sugar to prepare the body for sudden action. The outer part (cortex) secretes CORTICOSTEROIDS such as CORTISOL, which regulate the metabolism of carbohydrates, and mineral balance and the body's response to stress.

THE PANCREAS is a mixed gland: as an exocrine gland it makes digestive juice, and as an endocrine gland its ISLETS OF LANGERHANS secrete two hormones that control blood sugar. INSULIN (from beta cells) LOWERS blood glucose by helping cells absorb glucose and store it as glycogen; GLUCAGON (from alpha cells) RAISES blood glucose by breaking down stored glycogen. The two act antagonistically to keep blood sugar steady.

THE GONADS (sex glands) produce both gametes and sex hormones. The TESTES in males secrete TESTOSTERONE, which controls the development of male secondary sexual characters (such as beard, deep voice and muscular body) and sperm production. The OVARIES in females secrete OESTROGEN and PROGESTERONE, which control the development of female secondary sexual characters, the menstrual cycle and the maintenance of pregnancy.

17.9 HORMONAL DISORDERS

Because hormones are effective in tiny amounts, too little (hyposecretion) or too much (hypersecretion) of a hormone causes disorders. DIABETES MELLITUS results from a shortage of insulin (or the body's failure to respond to it): blood glucose rises and sugar appears in the urine; it is managed with a controlled diet and, when needed, insulin injections. GOITRE is the swelling of the thyroid gland caused by a lack of iodine in the diet, which prevents proper thyroxine formation; it is prevented by using iodised salt. A shortage of growth hormone in childhood causes DWARFISM (stunted growth with normal body proportions), while an excess of growth hormone in childhood causes GIGANTISM (abnormally tall stature); excess growth hormone in adults causes acromegaly (enlargement of the hands, feet and face). Under-secretion of thyroxine in children can also retard both physical and mental growth.

17.10 COMPARISON OF NERVOUS AND HORMONAL CONTROL

Both systems coordinate the body, but they differ in important ways. Nervous control uses ELECTRICAL impulses carried along neurons; hormonal control uses CHEMICAL messengers carried in the BLOOD. Nervous responses are VERY FAST and act on specific muscles or glands, but they are SHORT-LIVED. Hormonal responses are comparatively SLOW to begin, they are more widespread, and they are LONG-LASTING. The nervous message travels along a fixed pathway (nerve fibres) to a precise target, whereas a hormone travels everywhere in the blood but affects only its specific target organs. The two systems are closely linked: the hypothalamus of the brain controls the pituitary gland, so the nervous system and the endocrine system work together to keep the body coordinated.

SUMMARY

- Coordination links receptors to effectors so the body acts as one unit; it is carried out by the fast, electrical NERVOUS SYSTEM and the slower, chemical ENDOCRINE SYSTEM.
- The NEURON (nerve cell) is the unit of the nervous system, with a cell body, dendrites (receive impulses) and an axon (carries impulses away); many axons have an insulating MYELIN SHEATH broken at the nodes of Ranvier. Neurons are sensory, motor or interneurons and meet at SYNAPSES.
- A resting neuron is polarised (resting potential about -70 mV, kept by the sodium-potassium pump). A stimulus causes DEPOLARISATION (Na+ in, the ACTION POTENTIAL) followed by REPOLARISATION (K+ out). In myelinated fibres the impulse jumps node to node (SALTATORY CONDUCTION). Across a synapse the signal is carried by NEUROTRANSMITTERS and travels one way.
- The human nervous system = CENTRAL (brain + spinal cord) + PERIPHERAL. Brain parts: CEREBRUM (thinking, memory, voluntary action), CEREBELLUM (balance and coordination), MEDULLA OBLONGATA (heartbeat, breathing), THALAMUS (sensory relay) and HYPOTHALAMUS (temperature, hunger, thirst, links to pituitary). The PNS is somatic (voluntary) and autonomic (sympathetic 'fight-or-flight' vs parasympathetic 'rest-and-digest').
- A REFLEX ACTION is an automatic, involuntary response; its pathway (the REFLEX ARC) is receptor -> sensory neuron -> spinal cord (interneuron) -> motor neuron -> effector.
- Sense organs: the EYE (cornea, iris, pupil, lens, retina with rods and cones, optic nerve) forms an inverted image; the EAR (outer, middle with ossicles, inner cochlea and semicircular canals) serves hearing and balance.
- The ENDOCRINE SYSTEM uses ductless glands secreting HORMONES into the blood. Pituitary (MASTER GLAND, growth hormone), thyroid (THYROXINE, needs iodine), parathyroid (parathormone, calcium), adrenal (ADRENALINE for emergencies, cortisol), pancreas (INSULIN lowers and GLUCAGON raises blood sugar) and gonads (testosterone; oestrogen and progesterone).
- Hormonal disorders: DIABETES (insulin shortage), GOITRE (iodine deficiency), DWARFISM and GIGANTISM (too little or too much growth hormone).
- Nervous control is fast, electrical, short-lived and precise; hormonal control is slower, chemical, widespread and long-lasting. The hypothalamus links the two systems.

topics.name: The Neuron and Nerve Impulse
topics.description: The neuron as the unit of the nervous system (dendrites, cell body, axon, myelin sheath, synapse) and its types; the nerve impulse - resting potential, action potential, depolarisation, repolarisation, saltatory conduction - and synaptic transmission by neurotransmitters.

topics.name: The Central and Peripheral Nervous Systems
topics.description: The central nervous system (brain - cerebrum, cerebellum, medulla oblongata, thalamus, hypothalamus - and spinal cord) and the peripheral nervous system (somatic and autonomic, with sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions).

topics.name: Reflex Action and Sense Organs
topics.description: Reflex action as an automatic involuntary response and the components of the reflex arc; the structure and function of the sense organs, especially the eye and the ear.

topics.name: The Endocrine System and Hormones
topics.description: The endocrine system of ductless glands, the nature of hormones as chemical messengers carried in the blood, exocrine versus endocrine glands, and the general role of hormones in the body.

topics.name: Major Endocrine Glands and their Functions
topics.description: The chief endocrine glands and their hormones and functions: pituitary (master gland), thyroid (thyroxine), parathyroid, adrenal (adrenaline, cortisol), pancreas (insulin, glucagon) and gonads (testosterone, oestrogen, progesterone).

topics.name: Hormonal Disorders and Nervous vs Hormonal Control
topics.description: Common hormonal disorders (diabetes, goitre, dwarfism and gigantism) and a comparison of nervous control and hormonal control of the body.

learning_outcomes.topic_name: The Central and Peripheral Nervous Systems

Explain reflex action, trace the pathway of a reflex arc, and describe the structure and function of the sense organs, particularly the eye and the ear.
Describe the endocrine system and hormones, and distinguish exocrine from endocrine glands and their modes of action.

learning_outcomes.description: Analyse common hormonal disorders (diabetes, goitre, dwarfism and gigantism) and compare nervous control with hormonal control of the body.

chapter_summary.title: Coordination and Control - Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This NIOS Senior Secondary Biology summary explains how the body is coordinated by two systems: the fast electrical nervous system (neurons, brain, spinal cord, reflexes and sense organs) and the slower chemical endocrine system (ductless glands and their hormones), and compares the two.

branches.label: Neuron & Impulse
details: Parts: dendrites, cell body, axon, myelin sheath, synapse

branches.label: Peripheral NS & Reflex
details: Reflex arc: receptor -> sensory -> spinal cord -> motor -> effector

branches.label: Sense Organs
details: Eye: cornea, iris, pupil, lens, retina (rods, cones)

sections.heading: The neuron and the nerve impulse
bullets: A neuron has a cell body, dendrites that receive impulses and an axon that carries impulses away; many axons have a myelin sheath broken at nodes of Ranvier.
Neurons are sensory (receptor to CNS), motor (CNS to effector) or interneurons (connect the two); they meet at synapses.
A resting neuron is polarised (about -70 mV); a stimulus causes depolarisation (Na+ in, the action potential) then repolarisation (K+ out).
In myelinated fibres the impulse jumps node to node (saltatory conduction); across a synapse it is carried one-way by neurotransmitters.

sections.heading: The central and peripheral nervous systems
bullets: The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord; the peripheral nervous system is the cranial and spinal nerves.
Cerebrum controls thinking, memory and voluntary action; cerebellum controls balance and coordination; medulla oblongata controls heartbeat and breathing.
The thalamus relays sensations and the hypothalamus controls temperature, hunger, thirst and the pituitary gland.
The peripheral system is somatic (voluntary) and autonomic; the autonomic has sympathetic (fight-or-flight) and parasympathetic (rest-and-digest) divisions.

sections.heading: Reflex action and the sense organs
bullets: A reflex action is a rapid, automatic, involuntary response processed mainly in the spinal cord.
The reflex arc is: receptor -> sensory neuron -> spinal cord (interneuron) -> motor neuron -> effector.
In the eye, light passes through the cornea, pupil and lens to form an inverted image on the retina, whose rods and cones send impulses along the optic nerve.
In the ear, the outer ear collects sound, the middle-ear ossicles amplify it, and the inner-ear cochlea converts it to impulses; semicircular canals give balance.

sections.heading: The endocrine system and hormones
bullets: Endocrine glands are ductless and pour hormones directly into the blood, which carries them to target organs.
Exocrine glands (salivary, sweat) release secretions through ducts; endocrine glands do not.
Hormones are chemical messengers effective in tiny amounts that regulate growth, metabolism, reproduction and homeostasis.
Hormonal control is slower to start but more widespread and longer-lasting than nervous control.

sections.heading: Major glands, disorders and comparison
bullets: Pituitary (master gland, growth hormone), thyroid (thyroxine, needs iodine), adrenal (adrenaline), pancreas (insulin lowers, glucagon raises blood sugar), gonads (sex hormones).
Diabetes is caused by insulin shortage; goitre by iodine deficiency; dwarfism and gigantism by too little or too much growth hormone.
Nervous control is fast, electrical, precise and short-lived; hormonal control is slow, chemical, widespread and long-lasting.
The hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems, which work together to coordinate the body.

key_takeaways: Coordination links receptors to effectors through the fast electrical nervous system and the slower chemical endocrine system.
The neuron (dendrites, cell body, axon, myelin sheath) is the unit of the nervous system; neurons meet at synapses and are sensory, motor or interneurons.
The nerve impulse is an action potential: resting polarisation, depolarisation (Na+ in) and repolarisation (K+ out); myelinated fibres show fast saltatory conduction.
The CNS is brain plus spinal cord; the cerebrum thinks, the cerebellum balances, the medulla runs the heart and lungs, the hypothalamus links to the pituitary.
A reflex action follows the reflex arc through the spinal cord; the eye and ear are the main sense organs.
Key hormones: growth hormone (pituitary), thyroxine (thyroid), adrenaline (adrenal), insulin and glucagon (pancreas), and the sex hormones (gonads).
Diabetes, goitre and dwarfism/gigantism are hormonal disorders; nervous control is fast and short-lived while hormonal control is slow and long-lasting.

glossary.definition: The structural and functional unit of the nervous system, with a cell body, dendrites and an axon; it carries the nerve impulse.
The single long fibre of a neuron that carries impulses away from the cell body towards the next neuron or an effector.
A short, branched fibre of a neuron that receives impulses and carries them towards the cell body.
A fatty insulating layer around many axons, broken at the nodes of Ranvier, that speeds up impulse conduction.
The junction between two neurons (or a neuron and a muscle) across which impulses are passed chemically by neurotransmitters.
The potential difference (about -70 mV) across the membrane of a resting neuron, maintained by the sodium-potassium pump.
The rapid reversal of membrane charge (depolarisation) that constitutes the travelling nerve impulse.
The jumping of a nerve impulse from one node of Ranvier to the next in a myelinated fibre, making conduction faster.
A rapid, automatic, involuntary response to a stimulus, processed mainly in the spinal cord.
The nerve pathway of a reflex: receptor, sensory neuron, spinal cord (interneuron), motor neuron and effector.
A chemical messenger secreted in tiny amounts by an endocrine gland into the blood, which regulates a specific target organ.
A ductless gland that secretes its hormones directly into the blood, e.g. the thyroid, pituitary and adrenal glands.
The master endocrine gland at the base of the brain that secretes growth hormone and controls other glands.
A pancreatic hormone that lowers blood glucose; its shortage causes diabetes mellitus.
Swelling of the thyroid gland caused by a lack of iodine in the diet, preventing proper thyroxine formation.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Coordination and Control (NIOS Senior Secondary Biology)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Answer briefly and to the point; draw a labelled diagram where it helps. Marks are shown against each question.

questions.question: Define coordination. Name the two systems that bring about coordination in the human body.
questions.answer: Coordination is the process that links the activities of the different organs of the body so that they work together as one unit, connecting receptors to effectors so the correct response follows a stimulus. In humans it is brought about by two systems - the nervous system (fast, electrical control) and the endocrine system (slower, chemical control through hormones).
questions.explanation: Definition + the two control systems.

questions.question: Draw a labelled diagram of a neuron in words and state the function of the dendrites and the axon.
questions.answer: A neuron has three parts: a cell body (cyton) containing the nucleus, several short branched dendrites projecting from it, and a single long axon often covered by a myelin sheath with nodes of Ranvier, ending in axon terminals at a synapse. Function: the DENDRITES receive impulses and carry them towards the cell body, while the AXON carries impulses away from the cell body to the next neuron or to an effector.
questions.explanation: Parts named; dendrite receives, axon conducts away.

questions.question: Explain how a nerve impulse is generated and conducted along an axon, using the terms resting potential, depolarisation, repolarisation and saltatory conduction.
questions.answer: In a resting neuron the inside of the membrane is negative relative to the outside (about -70 mV), the RESTING POTENTIAL, maintained by the sodium-potassium pump that keeps Na+ outside and K+ inside; the membrane is polarised. When a stimulus reaches threshold, sodium channels open and Na+ rushes in, reversing the charge so the inside becomes positive - this is DEPOLARISATION, the action potential. Immediately afterwards potassium channels open, K+ moves out and the resting charge is restored - REPOLARISATION. The action potential passes as a wave along the axon because each depolarised patch triggers the next. In a myelinated axon the impulse cannot cross the insulating myelin, so it jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next; this jumping is SALTATORY CONDUCTION, which makes the impulse travel much faster.
questions.explanation: Resting -> depolarisation (Na+ in) -> repolarisation (K+ out); saltatory conduction in myelinated fibres.

questions.question: State the functions of the cerebrum, the cerebellum and the medulla oblongata.
questions.answer: Cerebrum: controls thinking, reasoning, memory, intelligence, will and voluntary actions, and interprets sensations from the sense organs. Cerebellum: maintains posture, balance and the precise coordination of muscular movements. Medulla oblongata: controls involuntary vital activities such as heartbeat, breathing, blood pressure, swallowing, coughing and vomiting.
questions.explanation: Three brain parts and their functions.

questions.question: What is a reflex action? Trace the path of the reflex arc when you touch a hot object.
questions.answer: A reflex action is a sudden, automatic, involuntary response to a stimulus that does not require conscious thought, e.g. pulling the hand away from a hot object. The impulse travels along the reflex arc: RECEPTOR in the skin detects the heat -> SENSORY NEURON carries the impulse to the spinal cord -> INTERNEURON in the spinal cord relays it -> MOTOR NEURON carries the response impulse -> EFFECTOR (arm muscle) contracts and withdraws the hand. Because it is processed in the spinal cord and not the brain, the response is very fast.
questions.explanation: Definition + receptor->sensory->spinal cord->motor->effector.

questions.question: Name the light-sensitive cells of the retina and state the role of each.
questions.answer: The retina contains two kinds of light-sensitive (photoreceptor) cells: RODS, which are sensitive in dim light and give black-and-white (night) vision, and CONES, which work in bright light and give colour vision. Both convert light into nerve impulses carried to the brain by the optic nerve.
questions.explanation: Rods (dim light/B&W) and cones (bright light/colour).

questions.question: Why is the pituitary gland called the master gland? Name one hormone it secretes.
questions.answer: The pituitary gland is called the master gland because its hormones control the activity of several other endocrine glands, such as the thyroid, adrenal cortex and gonads. One hormone it secretes is the growth hormone, which controls the growth of the body.
questions.explanation: Controls other glands; growth hormone.

questions.question: Explain how insulin and glucagon regulate blood glucose, and state what happens when insulin is deficient.
questions.answer: Insulin and glucagon are secreted by the islets of Langerhans of the pancreas and act antagonistically to keep blood glucose steady. When blood glucose rises (e.g. after a meal), INSULIN (from beta cells) helps body cells take up glucose and store it as glycogen, so blood glucose falls. When blood glucose falls (e.g. during fasting), GLUCAGON (from alpha cells) breaks down stored glycogen into glucose, so blood glucose rises. If insulin is deficient (or the body cannot respond to it), glucose is not taken up properly, blood glucose stays high and sugar appears in the urine - this disorder is DIABETES MELLITUS, managed by diet and, when needed, insulin injections.
questions.explanation: Insulin lowers, glucagon raises; deficiency -> diabetes.

questions.question: Name the disorder caused by (a) lack of iodine in the diet and (b) shortage of growth hormone in childhood.
questions.answer: (a) Lack of iodine in the diet prevents proper thyroxine formation and causes GOITRE, a swelling of the thyroid gland (prevented by using iodised salt). (b) A shortage of growth hormone in childhood causes DWARFISM, stunted growth with otherwise normal body proportions.
questions.explanation: Iodine lack -> goitre; low growth hormone -> dwarfism.

questions.question: Compare nervous control and hormonal control of the body under the headings type of message, speed, and duration of effect.
questions.answer: Type of message: nervous control uses electrical impulses carried along neurons, whereas hormonal control uses chemical messengers (hormones) carried in the blood. Speed: nervous responses are very fast (acting in a fraction of a second), whereas hormonal responses are comparatively slow to begin. Duration: nervous responses are short-lived, ending soon after the stimulus, whereas hormonal responses are widespread and long-lasting. In addition, a nerve impulse follows a fixed pathway to a precise target while a hormone travels everywhere in the blood but affects only its target organs. The two systems are linked because the hypothalamus of the brain controls the pituitary gland.
questions.explanation: Electrical vs chemical; fast vs slow; short-lived vs long-lasting.

questions.question: Name the three main parts of a neuron.
questions.answer: The three main parts of a neuron are: (1) the cell body (cyton/soma) containing the nucleus, (2) the dendrites - short branched fibres that receive impulses, and (3) the axon - a single long fibre that carries impulses away from the cell body.
questions.explanation: Cell body, dendrites, axon.

questions.question: Distinguish between a sensory neuron and a motor neuron.
questions.answer: A SENSORY (afferent) neuron carries impulses FROM the receptors (such as the skin, eye or ear) TO the central nervous system. A MOTOR (efferent) neuron carries impulses FROM the central nervous system TO the effectors (muscles and glands), which then produce the response. Interneurons within the CNS connect the two.
questions.explanation: Sensory: receptor to CNS; motor: CNS to effector.

questions.question: What is the myelin sheath and what is its function?
questions.answer: The myelin sheath is a fatty, insulating layer that wraps around many axons and is interrupted at intervals by gaps called the nodes of Ranvier. It insulates the axon and greatly increases the speed of impulse conduction, because the impulse jumps from node to node (saltatory conduction).
questions.explanation: Insulating fatty layer; speeds up conduction.

questions.question: Explain what is meant by resting potential and how it is maintained.
questions.answer: The resting potential is the potential difference (about -70 mV) across the membrane of a neuron that is not conducting an impulse, with the inside negative relative to the outside; the membrane is then said to be polarised. It is maintained by the sodium-potassium pump, which actively pushes sodium ions (Na+) out of the cell and potassium ions (K+) in, keeping the outside rich in Na+ and positively charged.
questions.explanation: -70 mV, polarised; maintained by the Na+/K+ pump.

questions.question: Describe how an impulse crosses a synapse.
questions.answer: When an impulse reaches the end of an axon it cannot leap the synaptic gap electrically. Instead, the impulse causes tiny vesicles in the axon ending to release chemical messengers called neurotransmitters (e.g. acetylcholine) into the synaptic cleft. The neurotransmitter diffuses across the gap and binds to receptors on the next neuron, generating a new impulse there. It is then broken down or reabsorbed. This makes transmission one-directional.
questions.explanation: Neurotransmitter released, diffuses, binds, regenerates impulse; one-way.

questions.question: Why does a nerve impulse travel faster in a myelinated axon than in a non-myelinated one?
questions.answer: In a myelinated axon the fatty myelin sheath insulates the fibre so the impulse cannot pass through the covered regions. It therefore jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next - a process called saltatory conduction. Because the impulse leaps over the insulated stretches instead of moving continuously along the whole membrane, it covers the distance much faster than in a non-myelinated axon, where the impulse must travel continuously.
questions.explanation: Saltatory (node-to-node) conduction is faster than continuous conduction.

questions.question: Name the two main divisions of the human nervous system.
questions.answer: The two main divisions are the CENTRAL nervous system (CNS), made of the brain and the spinal cord, and the PERIPHERAL nervous system (PNS), made of the cranial and spinal nerves that connect the CNS to the rest of the body.
questions.explanation: Central (brain + spinal cord) and peripheral.

questions.question: State the functions of the hypothalamus and the thalamus.
questions.answer: The HYPOTHALAMUS controls body temperature, hunger, thirst, sleep and emotions, and it links the nervous system to the endocrine system by controlling the pituitary gland. The THALAMUS acts as a relay centre that passes incoming sensory impulses on to the cerebrum.
questions.explanation: Hypothalamus: temperature/hunger/thirst + controls pituitary; thalamus: sensory relay.

questions.question: Distinguish between the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions of the autonomic nervous system.
questions.answer: Both are parts of the autonomic nervous system and act antagonistically. The SYMPATHETIC division prepares the body for emergency 'fight-or-flight' situations - it speeds up the heartbeat, widens the pupils, raises blood pressure and diverts blood to the muscles. The PARASYMPATHETIC division restores calm 'rest-and-digest' conditions - it slows the heartbeat, constricts the pupils and promotes digestion.
questions.explanation: Sympathetic = fight-or-flight; parasympathetic = rest-and-digest.

questions.question: List, in order, the components of a reflex arc.
questions.answer: The components of a reflex arc, in order, are: (1) RECEPTOR - detects the stimulus; (2) SENSORY (afferent) NEURON - carries the impulse to the spinal cord; (3) INTERNEURON in the spinal cord - relays the impulse; (4) MOTOR (efferent) NEURON - carries the response impulse; and (5) EFFECTOR - a muscle or gland that produces the response.
questions.explanation: Receptor -> sensory neuron -> interneuron (spinal cord) -> motor neuron -> effector.

questions.question: Describe how an image is formed in the eye.
questions.answer: Light from an object enters the eye through the transparent cornea and passes through the pupil, whose size is adjusted by the iris to control the amount of light. The lens focuses the light onto the retina at the back of the eye, forming a small, inverted, real image. The light-sensitive rods and cones of the retina convert the light into nerve impulses, which travel along the optic nerve to the cerebrum, where the image is interpreted the right way up.
questions.explanation: Cornea/pupil/iris -> lens focuses -> inverted image on retina -> optic nerve -> brain.

questions.question: Describe the path of sound through the three parts of the ear.
questions.answer: The OUTER EAR (pinna and ear canal) collects sound waves and directs them onto the eardrum, which vibrates. The MIDDLE EAR contains three ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) that amplify these vibrations and pass them to the inner ear. The INNER EAR contains the fluid-filled cochlea, whose receptor cells convert the vibrations into nerve impulses that travel along the auditory nerve to the brain for hearing.
questions.explanation: Outer ear collects -> middle-ear ossicles amplify -> inner-ear cochlea -> auditory nerve.

questions.question: Distinguish between exocrine and endocrine glands.
questions.answer: EXOCRINE glands (such as salivary and sweat glands) release their secretions through ducts onto a surface or into a cavity. ENDOCRINE glands are ductless and release their secretions (hormones) directly into the blood, which carries them to distant target organs.
questions.explanation: Exocrine: with ducts; endocrine: ductless, into blood.

questions.question: What is a hormone? State two features of hormones.
questions.answer: A hormone is a chemical messenger secreted in tiny amounts by an endocrine gland directly into the blood, which regulates the activity of specific target cells or organs. Features: (1) they are effective in very small (trace) amounts; (2) they are carried by the blood and act on specific target organs, regulating growth, metabolism, reproduction and internal balance; their effects are slow to start but long-lasting.
questions.explanation: Chemical messenger in blood; small amounts, target-specific, long-lasting.

questions.question: Name the hormones secreted by the pancreas and state their source within it.
questions.answer: The pancreas, through its islets of Langerhans, secretes two hormones that control blood sugar: INSULIN (from the beta cells) and GLUCAGON (from the alpha cells).
questions.explanation: Insulin (beta cells) and glucagon (alpha cells).

questions.question: Name the two parts of the adrenal gland and the hormones each secretes.
questions.answer: The adrenal gland has two parts. The inner part (medulla) secretes ADRENALINE (epinephrine), the emergency 'fight-or-flight' hormone that raises heartbeat, breathing rate and blood sugar. The outer part (cortex) secretes corticosteroids such as CORTISOL, which regulate carbohydrate metabolism, mineral balance and the response to stress.
questions.explanation: Medulla: adrenaline; cortex: cortisol/corticosteroids.

questions.question: Name the endocrine gland for each: (a) master gland, (b) hormone containing iodine, (c) regulates blood calcium.
questions.answer: (a) The master gland is the PITUITARY gland, which controls other endocrine glands. (b) The iodine-containing hormone thyroxine is secreted by the THYROID gland. (c) Blood calcium is regulated by parathormone from the PARATHYROID glands.
questions.explanation: Pituitary; thyroid; parathyroid.

questions.question: Explain how the body responds to sudden danger through a hormone.
questions.answer: When a person faces sudden danger or fright, the adrenal medulla releases the hormone ADRENALINE into the blood. Adrenaline prepares the body for immediate 'fight-or-flight' action: it speeds up the heartbeat and breathing, raises blood pressure and blood sugar (by releasing glucose), and diverts blood to the muscles. These changes give the body extra energy and alertness to face the emergency.
questions.explanation: Adrenaline surge: faster heart/breathing, more blood sugar, energy for action.

questions.question: Why must a diabetic person sometimes be given insulin injections?
questions.answer: In diabetes mellitus the pancreas does not make enough insulin (or the body cannot respond to it), so blood glucose cannot be taken up by cells and rises to high levels, spilling into the urine. Giving insulin by injection replaces the missing hormone, helping the cells take up glucose and bringing blood sugar back to normal.
questions.explanation: Insulin is deficient, so it is supplied to lower blood glucose.

questions.question: A child grows abnormally tall for their age. Which gland and hormone might be responsible, and why?
questions.answer: This suggests the PITUITARY gland is secreting too much GROWTH HORMONE during childhood. Growth hormone controls the growth of the body; an excess in childhood, while the long bones can still grow, produces abnormally tall stature - a condition called GIGANTISM. (Too little growth hormone in childhood would instead cause dwarfism.)
questions.explanation: Excess growth hormone from the pituitary -> gigantism.

questions.question: Give three differences between nervous control and hormonal control.
questions.answer: (1) Nature of message: nervous control uses electrical impulses along neurons, while hormonal control uses chemical messengers (hormones) in the blood. (2) Speed: nervous responses are very fast, while hormonal responses are slower to begin. (3) Duration: nervous responses are short-lived, while hormonal responses are widespread and long-lasting. (Also: a nerve impulse follows a fixed path to a precise target, whereas a hormone travels in the blood to specific target organs.)
questions.explanation: Electrical vs chemical; fast vs slow; short-lived vs long-lasting.

questions.question: Name any two hormonal disorders and state their cause.
questions.answer: (1) DIABETES MELLITUS - caused by a shortage of the hormone insulin, so blood glucose rises. (2) GOITRE - caused by a deficiency of iodine in the diet, which prevents proper formation of thyroxine and causes the thyroid gland to swell. (Dwarfism/gigantism from too little/too much growth hormone are other examples.)
questions.explanation: Diabetes: insulin shortage; goitre: iodine deficiency.

questions.question: Describe the structure of a neuron and explain the function of each part.
questions.answer: A neuron (nerve cell) is the structural and functional unit of the nervous system and has three main parts. (1) The CELL BODY (cyton or soma) contains the nucleus and cytoplasm with organelles including Nissl granules; it carries out the metabolic activities of the cell and processes incoming signals. (2) DENDRITES are short, branched fibres projecting from the cell body; they RECEIVE impulses from receptors or other neurons and carry them TOWARDS the cell body. (3) The AXON is a single long fibre that carries impulses AWAY from the cell body to the next neuron or an effector; it may be wrapped in an insulating MYELIN SHEATH broken at the NODES OF RANVIER, which speeds conduction, and it ends in fine terminals that form a SYNAPSE with the next cell. Supporting neuroglia nourish and protect neurons. According to function, neurons are sensory (receptor to CNS), motor (CNS to effector) or interneurons (linking the two).
questions.explanation: Cell body (nucleus), dendrites (receive), axon (conduct away), myelin/nodes (speed), synapse (junction).

questions.question: Explain the generation and conduction of a nerve impulse, and how it is transmitted across a synapse.
questions.answer: A resting neuron is POLARISED: the inside of its membrane is about -70 mV relative to the outside (the RESTING POTENTIAL), maintained by the sodium-potassium pump that keeps Na+ outside and K+ inside. When a stimulus reaches threshold, sodium channels open and Na+ rushes in, so the inside briefly becomes positive - this reversal is DEPOLARISATION and constitutes the ACTION POTENTIAL. Potassium channels then open, K+ flows out, and the resting charge is restored (REPOLARISATION). Each depolarised patch triggers the next, so the impulse travels along the axon without weakening; it obeys the all-or-none law. In myelinated fibres the impulse jumps node to node (SALTATORY CONDUCTION), which is faster. At the end of the axon the impulse reaches a SYNAPSE. Because it cannot cross the gap electrically, vesicles release NEUROTRANSMITTERS (e.g. acetylcholine) into the synaptic cleft; these diffuse across and bind to receptors on the next neuron, starting a fresh impulse. The transmitter is then removed, and transmission is one-directional.
questions.explanation: Resting -> depolarisation -> repolarisation; saltatory conduction; synapse via neurotransmitters, one-way.

questions.question: Describe the main parts of the human brain and their functions.
questions.answer: The brain, protected by the skull, meninges and cerebrospinal fluid, has three regions. The FOREBRAIN is dominated by the CEREBRUM, the largest part, whose folded cortex controls thinking, memory, reasoning, intelligence, will, voluntary actions and interpretation of sensations. Within it lie the THALAMUS, which relays sensory impulses to the cerebrum, and the HYPOTHALAMUS, which controls temperature, hunger, thirst, sleep and emotions and governs the pituitary gland, thus linking the nervous and endocrine systems. The MIDBRAIN connects the fore- and hindbrain and handles some eye and ear reflexes. The HINDBRAIN contains the CEREBELLUM, which maintains posture, balance and precise muscular coordination, and the MEDULLA OBLONGATA, which controls involuntary vital activities such as heartbeat, breathing, blood pressure, swallowing and coughing.
questions.explanation: Cerebrum (higher functions), thalamus (relay), hypothalamus (temp/pituitary), cerebellum (balance), medulla (vital functions).

questions.question: What is a reflex action? Describe the reflex arc with a suitable example and explain why the response is so fast.
questions.answer: A reflex action is a sudden, automatic, involuntary response to a stimulus that does not need conscious thought - for example withdrawing the hand at once from a hot object, or blinking when something nears the eye. The nerve pathway of a reflex is the REFLEX ARC. Taking the hot-object example: the RECEPTORS in the skin detect the heat; a SENSORY NEURON carries the impulse to the SPINAL CORD; an INTERNEURON there relays it directly to a MOTOR NEURON; the motor neuron carries the response impulse to the EFFECTOR (the arm muscle), which contracts and pulls the hand away. Because the impulse is processed in the spinal cord and not sent up to the brain for a decision, the pathway is very short and the response occurs in a fraction of a second; the brain is informed only afterwards, which is why we feel the pain just after the hand has moved. This speed protects the body from injury.
questions.explanation: Definition; receptor->sensory->spinal cord->motor->effector; short spinal path = very fast, protective.

questions.question: What is the endocrine system? Explain how hormones act and how endocrine glands differ from exocrine glands.
questions.answer: The endocrine system is the body's chemical control system, made up of ductless glands that secrete chemical messengers called HORMONES directly into the blood. The blood carries each hormone throughout the body, but it acts only on its specific TARGET organ, where it regulates activities such as growth, metabolism, reproduction and internal balance (homeostasis). Hormones are effective in very small amounts; their effects are slower to begin than nervous responses but are more widespread and longer-lasting. ENDOCRINE glands (thyroid, pituitary, adrenal, etc.) are DUCTLESS and pour hormones into the blood, whereas EXOCRINE glands (salivary, sweat glands) have DUCTS through which they release their secretions onto a surface or into a cavity. Some glands, like the pancreas, are mixed - both exocrine and endocrine.
questions.explanation: Ductless glands, hormones into blood to target organs; endocrine ductless vs exocrine with ducts.

questions.question: Name the major endocrine glands of the human body and state one important hormone and function of each.
questions.answer: The major endocrine glands and their hormones are: (1) PITUITARY (master gland) - secretes GROWTH HORMONE, controlling body growth, and directs other glands. (2) THYROID - secretes THYROXINE (contains iodine), controlling the rate of metabolism, growth and development. (3) PARATHYROID - secretes PARATHORMONE, regulating blood calcium and phosphorus. (4) ADRENAL - the medulla secretes ADRENALINE, the emergency hormone that raises heartbeat and blood sugar, and the cortex secretes cortisol. (5) PANCREAS - its islets secrete INSULIN (lowers blood glucose) and GLUCAGON (raises it). (6) GONADS - the testes secrete TESTOSTERONE (male characters) and the ovaries secrete OESTROGEN and PROGESTERONE (female characters and reproductive cycle).
questions.explanation: Pituitary/GH, thyroid/thyroxine, parathyroid/parathormone, adrenal/adrenaline, pancreas/insulin-glucagon, gonads/sex hormones.

questions.question: Explain, with examples, how hormones regulate blood glucose and how the body prepares for an emergency.
questions.answer: BLOOD GLUCOSE: The pancreas keeps blood sugar steady using two antagonistic hormones from its islets of Langerhans. After a meal, when glucose rises, INSULIN (from beta cells) makes body cells take up glucose and store it as glycogen, so blood glucose falls. During fasting or exercise, when glucose falls, GLUCAGON (from alpha cells) breaks stored glycogen back into glucose, so blood glucose rises. If insulin is lacking, glucose stays high and diabetes results. EMERGENCY: When the body faces sudden danger, the adrenal medulla releases ADRENALINE (the 'fight-or-flight' hormone). It speeds up heartbeat and breathing, raises blood pressure, releases extra glucose into the blood for energy and diverts blood to the muscles - preparing the body to fight or flee. These examples show how specific hormones are precisely matched to the body processes they regulate.
questions.explanation: Insulin lowers/glucagon raises glucose (antagonistic); adrenaline drives fight-or-flight.

questions.question: Discuss the common hormonal disorders and compare nervous control with hormonal control of the body.
questions.answer: HORMONAL DISORDERS: (1) DIABETES MELLITUS results from a shortage of insulin, so blood glucose rises and sugar appears in the urine; it is managed by diet and insulin injections. (2) GOITRE is a swelling of the thyroid caused by iodine deficiency, which prevents thyroxine formation; it is prevented by iodised salt. (3) DWARFISM results from too little growth hormone in childhood (stunted growth), while GIGANTISM results from too much growth hormone in childhood (abnormally tall stature). COMPARISON: Nervous control uses ELECTRICAL impulses carried along neurons, is VERY FAST, acts on precise targets and is SHORT-LIVED. Hormonal control uses CHEMICAL messengers carried in the BLOOD, is SLOWER to start, is more WIDESPREAD and is LONG-LASTING. The two systems are closely linked, since the hypothalamus of the brain controls the pituitary gland, so together they coordinate the body.
questions.explanation: Diabetes/goitre/dwarfism-gigantism; nervous (electrical, fast, short) vs hormonal (chemical, slow, long); linked by hypothalamus.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The nervous system is built from cells called neurons. A neuron has a cell body with a nucleus, several dendrites, and a single long axon that is often covered by a myelin sheath interrupted by gaps. Where one neuron meets the next, there is a tiny gap.
(a) Which part of the neuron receives impulses?
(b) Name the covering of the axon and its function.
(c) What are the gaps in this covering called?
(d) Name the junction between two neurons.
questions.answer:
(a) The DENDRITES receive impulses and carry them towards the cell body.
(b) The covering is the MYELIN SHEATH; it insulates the axon and speeds up impulse conduction.
(c) The gaps are the NODES OF RANVIER.
(d) The junction between two neurons is the SYNAPSE.
questions.explanation: Dendrites receive; myelin insulates/speeds; nodes of Ranvier; synapse.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A resting neuron has a potential of about -70 mV, with the inside negative. When stimulated, sodium ions rush in and the charge reverses; soon after, potassium ions move out and the resting state returns. In myelinated fibres the impulse jumps between nodes.
(a) What is the -70 mV state called?
(b) Name the process when sodium ions rush in.
(c) Name the process when potassium ions move out.
(d) What is the jumping conduction called, and what is its advantage?
questions.answer:
(a) The -70 mV state is the RESTING POTENTIAL (the membrane is polarised), maintained by the sodium-potassium pump.
(b) The rush of Na+ inward, reversing the charge, is DEPOLARISATION (it produces the action potential).
(c) The outward movement of K+ that restores the resting charge is REPOLARISATION.
(d) The jumping between nodes of Ranvier is SALTATORY CONDUCTION; its advantage is that the impulse travels much faster than in a non-myelinated fibre.
questions.explanation: Resting potential; depolarisation; repolarisation; saltatory conduction = faster.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The human brain has several parts. One large folded part governs thought and voluntary action; another at the back controls balance; a lower part controls the heartbeat and breathing; and a small region controls body temperature and the pituitary gland.
(a) Name the part that controls thinking and voluntary action.
(b) Which part controls balance and coordination?
(c) Which part controls heartbeat and breathing?
(d) Which part controls body temperature and the pituitary gland?
questions.answer:
(a) The CEREBRUM controls thinking, memory and voluntary action.
(b) The CEREBELLUM controls balance, posture and coordination of movements.
(c) The MEDULLA OBLONGATA controls heartbeat, breathing and other involuntary vital activities.
(d) The HYPOTHALAMUS controls body temperature (and hunger, thirst) and governs the pituitary gland, linking the nervous and endocrine systems.
questions.explanation: Cerebrum; cerebellum; medulla oblongata; hypothalamus.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
When a person accidentally touches a hot plate, the hand is pulled away instantly, before the pain is even felt. This is an automatic response processed in the spinal cord along a fixed pathway.
(a) What is this type of response called?
(b) Name, in order, the parts of the pathway involved.
(c) Why is the hand withdrawn before the pain is felt?
(d) State one value of such responses to the body.
questions.answer:
(a) It is a REFLEX ACTION - a sudden, automatic, involuntary response.
(b) The pathway (reflex arc) is: receptor in the skin -> sensory neuron -> spinal cord (interneuron) -> motor neuron -> effector (arm muscle).
(c) The impulse is processed in the spinal cord and the response is sent to the muscle at once, while the message reaches the brain (where pain is felt) only afterwards; so the hand moves before the pain is registered.
(d) Reflexes are very fast and protect the body from harm or injury.
questions.explanation: Reflex action; receptor->sensory->spinal cord->motor->effector; spinal processing is faster than brain; protective.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The eye is the organ of sight. Light passes through the transparent front, then through an opening whose size is controlled by a coloured ring, and is focused by a lens onto a light-sensitive layer at the back that contains two kinds of cells.
(a) Name the transparent front part of the eye.
(b) Name the coloured ring and the opening it controls.
(c) Name the light-sensitive layer and its two cell types.
(d) Which nerve carries impulses from the eye to the brain?
questions.answer:
(a) The transparent front part is the CORNEA.
(b) The coloured ring is the IRIS; it controls the size of the PUPIL, the opening through which light enters.
(c) The light-sensitive layer is the RETINA; its two cell types are RODS (dim-light, black-and-white vision) and CONES (bright-light, colour vision).
(d) The OPTIC NERVE carries impulses from the eye to the brain.
questions.explanation: Cornea; iris/pupil; retina with rods and cones; optic nerve.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The body has two kinds of glands. Some, like the salivary and sweat glands, release their products through ducts. Others, like the thyroid and pituitary, are ductless and pour chemical messengers straight into the blood, which carries them to particular organs.
(a) What name is given to the ductless glands?
(b) What are the chemical messengers called?
(c) Give one example each of an exocrine and an endocrine gland.
(d) How do these messengers reach their target organ?
questions.answer:
(a) The ductless glands are ENDOCRINE glands.
(b) The chemical messengers are HORMONES.
(c) Exocrine gland: salivary (or sweat) gland; endocrine gland: thyroid (or pituitary).
(d) They are released into the BLOOD, which transports them to their specific target organs.
questions.explanation: Endocrine glands; hormones; salivary vs thyroid; carried by blood.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The pancreas is a mixed gland. As an endocrine gland its islets of Langerhans secrete two hormones with opposite effects on blood sugar. One is released when blood sugar is high, the other when it is low.
(a) Name the two hormones secreted by the islets of Langerhans.
(b) Which hormone is released when blood sugar is high, and what does it do?
(c) Which hormone is released when blood sugar is low, and what does it do?
(d) Why is the pancreas called a mixed gland?
questions.answer:
(a) The two hormones are INSULIN and GLUCAGON.
(b) INSULIN is released when blood sugar is high; it helps cells take up glucose and store it as glycogen, LOWERING blood sugar.
(c) GLUCAGON is released when blood sugar is low; it breaks down stored glycogen into glucose, RAISING blood sugar.
(d) The pancreas is a mixed gland because it acts both as an exocrine gland (making digestive juice through a duct) and as an endocrine gland (secreting insulin and glucagon into the blood).
questions.explanation: Insulin and glucagon; insulin lowers, glucagon raises; mixed = exocrine + endocrine.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A student sitting for an examination suddenly feels their heart pounding, breathing quicken and hands become alert as they see the question paper. Their adrenal glands have released a hormone into the blood.
(a) Name the hormone responsible and the gland part that secretes it.
(b) List two body changes it brings about.
(c) By what popular name is this response known?
(d) Is this an example of nervous or hormonal control? Give a reason.
questions.answer:
(a) The hormone is ADRENALINE (epinephrine), secreted by the medulla (inner part) of the adrenal gland.
(b) It speeds up the heartbeat and breathing, raises blood pressure and blood sugar, and diverts blood to the muscles (any two).
(c) It is known as the 'fight-or-flight' (emergency) response.
(d) It is an example of HORMONAL control, because the response is brought about by a chemical (adrenaline) carried in the blood; however, it works closely with the nervous system, which triggers the release.
questions.explanation: Adrenaline from adrenal medulla; faster heart/breathing; fight-or-flight; hormonal (chemical in blood).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Hormones must be secreted in the right amounts. Too little insulin causes one disorder; a lack of iodine in the diet causes another; and abnormal secretion of growth hormone in childhood causes two more.
(a) Name the disorder caused by too little insulin.
(b) Name the disorder caused by iodine deficiency and how it can be prevented.
(c) Name the disorder caused by too little growth hormone in childhood.
(d) Name the disorder caused by too much growth hormone in childhood.
questions.answer:
(a) Too little insulin causes DIABETES MELLITUS (blood glucose rises and sugar appears in the urine).
(b) Iodine deficiency causes GOITRE (swelling of the thyroid); it can be prevented by using iodised salt.
(c) Too little growth hormone in childhood causes DWARFISM (stunted growth with normal proportions).
(d) Too much growth hormone in childhood causes GIGANTISM (abnormally tall stature).
questions.explanation: Diabetes; goitre (iodised salt); dwarfism; gigantism.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The body is coordinated by two systems. One sends rapid electrical signals along nerve fibres to precise targets, and its effects are short-lived. The other sends chemical messengers through the blood; its effects are slower to appear but are widespread and last longer. A region of the brain links the two.
(a) Name the two systems described.
(b) State the type of message each uses.
(c) Compare the speed and duration of their effects.
(d) Name the brain region that links the two systems.
questions.answer:
(a) The two systems are the NERVOUS system and the ENDOCRINE (hormonal) system.
(b) The nervous system uses electrical impulses (along neurons); the endocrine system uses chemical messengers (hormones) carried in the blood.
(c) Nervous effects are very fast but short-lived; hormonal effects are slower to begin but widespread and long-lasting.
(d) The HYPOTHALAMUS links the two systems, because it controls the pituitary gland.
questions.explanation: Nervous vs endocrine; electrical vs chemical; fast/short vs slow/long; hypothalamus links them.
